turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: My avó's house, my grandmother's, near Ponte de Lima, up in the Minho. I'm talking the seventies, when I was a boy. Granite, all of it. Two floors, and the animals lived downstairs, in the corte, the cow stable. Two cows. And the adega next to it, the wine cellar, with the barrels.

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Stone stairs on the outside, at the front, going up to the varanda. Granite steps, no handrail, worn down in the middle. The varanda had the vine over it, the ramada, the grapes hanging down over your head.

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: From the varanda one door went straight into the kitchen, the cozinha. That door faced south, you had sun all afternoon. The lareira, the open fireplace, was on the right wall, no, sorry, facing you as you came in, on the back wall, with the black iron pot hanging over it. Everything black from the smoke. A long table and two benches.

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Two, off the kitchen, on your left as you come in. Mine and my avó's. My avô had died already by then. An iron bed in each. The arca, the big wooden chest, at the foot of hers. And the oratório, the little cabinet for the saint, on the wall in her room.

turns.speaker: B
turns.transcript: What was outside, around the house?

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: The eira, the threshing floor, flat granite in front of the house, where we dried the corn. And the espigueiro at the edge of it, the granary on stone legs, so the rats couldn't climb up. Every house up there has one.

turns.speaker: A
turns.transcript: Yes, the forno, inside the kitchen, in the corner beside the lareira. Big enough that a child could crawl inside, and I did, once, when it was cold. Only once. The kitchen was maybe five metres by four.
